lead: A differential pair is two matched transistors with emitters, or sources, joined and fed by one constant tail current IEE. Inputs v1 and v2 steer that fixed current: raise v1 and Q1 takes more, Q2 less; the sum stays IEE. The output depends on vid = v1 − v2, not on the average (v1 + v2)/2. That is why the pair sits at every op-amp input: it amplifies the wanted difference and rejects hum and noise common to both wires. Rejection is covered in 5.2.
prereq: You need Unit 2, Transistor Biasing and Small-Signal Amplifiers — the DC operating point, gm = IC/VT for a BJT, gm = 2ID/VOV for a MOSFET, and CE and CS gain expressions.

sections.h3: Two matched devices sharing one tail current

blocks.text: Take two identical BJTs Q1 and Q2. Join their emitters to a current source IEE sinking to −VEE. Connect collectors to VCC through equal RC. Drive bases from v1 and v2. The MOSFET version is identical: sources joined, tail IEE to ground or −VSS, drains to VDD through equal RD.
Define vid = v1 − v2 (difference input, volts) and vicm = (v1 + v2)/2 (common-mode input, volts). Then v1 = vicm + vid/2 and v2 = vicm − vid/2.
At vid = 0 both devices have the same VBE or VGS, so they split the tail equally: IC1 = IC2 = IEE/2. Collector voltages are equal, VC = VCC − (IEE/2)RC, and the output difference is zero.
Raise v1 and lower v2: Q1 needs more current, Q2 less. The tail holds the total at IEE, so Q1's gain is Q2's loss. The input difference decides the split; the tail decides only the sum.

sections.h3: Small signals: each device gets half the difference

blocks.text: For small vid the joined node does not move; each base-emitter voltage changes by vid/2 with opposite signs. So ΔIC1 = +gm vid/2 and ΔIC2 = −gm vid/2.
vod = vC1 − vC2 = −gm RC vid,   Ad = vod/vid = −gm RC
blocks.where: vod is the differential output voltage between collectors, in volts; gm is transconductance in siemens; RC is collector resistance in ohms; vid is differential input in volts. The minus sign means output falls when v1 rises.

blocks.text: Single-collector gain is half: Av1 = vc1/vid = −gm RC/2. A differential output doubles it and cancels shared components.

blocks.where: IC and ID are DC currents at balance, IEE/2, in amperes; VT = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at room temperature; VOV = VGS − VTH is overdrive voltage in volts; µn is electron mobility, Cox gate capacitance per unit area, W/L channel width-to-length ratio.

blocks.text: With IEE/2, BJT gm = IEE/(2VT) and MOSFET gm = IEE/VOV. The tail current sets gain, so a current mirror usually biases the pair (5.3).

sections.h3: The joined node: virtual ground or follower

blocks.text: Differential signals move v1 up and v2 down equally. Q1 pushes current into the joined node while Q2 pulls the same out, so its voltage does not change. For vid the emitter or source is a virtual ground, and each half is a CE or CS stage of gain gm RC.

Common-mode signals move both inputs together. Both devices try to conduct more; the tail source resists with high output resistance REE. The joined node follows the input like a follower, so VBE and collector currents barely change. Common-mode gain is small, about −RC/(2REE) for a BJT pair, against −gm RC for differential gain.
A current-source tail is the point: a resistor tail changes current when common-mode voltage changes, but a good current source holds current almost constant. The gain ratio is CMRR, covered in 5.2.
On the bench, a BJT pair's joined node sits about VBE (0.7 V) below the input DC level; a MOSFET pair's sits about VGS below it.

items: Every op-amp and comparator input stage is a differential pair, the first block in 5.5.
Balanced audio and instrumentation cables: hum couples equally onto both wires and is rejected as common mode.
High-speed serial links such as USB and HDMI drive and receive data differentially, so supply noise disturbs both wires and cancels.

figure.caption: A fixed tail current is split between two matched devices; the input difference decides the split, and the collector or drain resistors turn the split into a voltage. Notice that the tail sets the total and never the difference.

spec.title: Differential pair: current steering
spec.aria: Block diagram: a tail current source biases a matched pair; the input difference steers the tail current between the two devices to form the output.

examples.question: A BJT differential pair has IEE = 1 mA, VCC = 12 V, RC = 5 kΩ on each collector, and VT = 26 mV. β is very large. (a) Find IC1 and IC2 at vid = 0. (b) Find gm and the single-ended differential gain at collector 1. (c) For vid = 5 mV, find vC1, vC2 and the differential output voltage.
steps: At vid = 0 the pair is balanced: IC1 = IC2 = IEE/2 = 1 mA / 2 = 0.5 mA. With large β, IC ≈ IE.
Single-ended gain at collector 1: |Av1| = gm RC/2 = 19.23 mS × 5 kΩ / 2 = 96.15 / 2 = 48.08. A rising v1 turns Q1 on harder and drops vC1, so Av1 = −48.08, about 33.6 dB.
For vid = 5 mV, ΔIC1 = gm vid/2 = 19.23 mS × 5 mV / 2 = 48.08 µA and ΔIC2 = −48.08 µA. So IC1 = 0.5 mA + 0.0481 mA = 0.5481 mA and IC2 = 0.5 mA − 0.0481 mA = 0.4519 mA.
vod = vC1 − vC2 = 9.2596 − 9.7404 = −0.4808 V. Check: −gm RC vid = −19.23 mS × 5 kΩ × 5 mV = −0.4808 V. 5 mV is well below 2VT = 52 mV, so the linear estimate is good to a few percent.
examples.answer: IC1 = IC2 = 0.5 mA at balance; gm = 19.23 mS; single-ended gain at collector 1 = −48.08 and differential gain = −96.15; at vid = 5 mV, vC1 = 9.2596 V, vC2 = 9.7404 V and vod = −0.4808 V.

traps: Using IC = IEE instead of IEE/2 at balance. Each device carries only half the tail current.
Dropping the 1/2 in a single-ended output. Gain at one collector or drain is gm RC/2; a differential output gives the full gm RC.
Treating the joined node as a virtual ground for common-mode signals. It is a virtual ground only for vid; for vicm it follows the input like a follower.
Sign confusion: a rising v1 raises IC1, so vC1 falls. Collector 1 is the inverting output; collector 2 is non-inverting.
Using the small-signal formula for large vid. Once vid approaches a few times VT (or VOV for a MOSFET), one device takes nearly all of IEE and output flattens at IEE·RC; gm is no longer constant.

quiz.q: In a matched BJT differential pair with tail current IEE and very large β, what is each collector current at vid = 0?
quiz.a: IC1 = IC2 = IEE/2, because matched devices share the fixed tail current equally. For IEE = 1 mA that is 0.5 mA each.

quiz.q: Define vid and vicm for inputs v1 and v2, and write v1 and v2 in terms of them.
quiz.a: vid = v1 − v2 and vicm = (v1 + v2)/2, both in volts; then v1 = vicm + vid/2 and v2 = vicm − vid/2.

quiz.q: Why does a current-source tail reject common-mode signals better than a resistor tail?
quiz.a: A current source holds IEE almost constant when the joined-node voltage moves, so common-mode input only shifts that node and hardly changes IC. A resistor tail lets current rise with common-mode voltage, giving much larger common-mode gain.

quiz.q: A MOSFET differential pair has IEE = 200 µA, RD = 10 kΩ per drain, and VOV = 0.2 V for each device. Find gm and the differential gain.
quiz.a: Each drain carries ID = IEE/2 = 100 µA. gm = 2ID/VOV = 2 × 100 µA / 0.2 V = 1 mS. Differential gain Ad = −gm RD = −1 mS × 10 kΩ = −10, that is 20 dB.

quiz.q: Using the BJT pair of the worked example (IEE = 1 mA, RC = 5 kΩ, VT = 26 mV, gm = 19.23 mS), estimate the differential output for vid = 10 mV and state whether the small-signal answer is trustworthy.
quiz.a: vod = −gm RC vid = −19.23 mS × 5 kΩ × 10 mV = −0.96 V. The linear estimate holds because 10 mV is about 0.2 × 2VT = 52 mV; beyond that the true curve bends and the magnitude is smaller.

quiz.q: Both inputs of a BJT pair rise by 1 V together while the tail current source stays ideal. Describe what happens at the emitter node and at the output.
quiz.a: This is pure common-mode input. The emitter node rises by almost 1 V, following the input, so VBE and both collector currents stay nearly unchanged. Output moves only by common-mode gain, roughly RC/(2REE) times 1 V, a few millivolts.

quiz.q: A student applies 2 V DC to both inputs of a matched pair and measures zero volts between the collectors. Is the circuit faulty? Explain.
quiz.a: Not faulty. Both inputs at 2 V is pure common-mode input, and a matched pair with a good tail source rejects it, so collector currents stay at IEE/2 and collector voltages stay equal. A nonzero reading would come from device mismatch or finite tail resistance, studied in 5.2.

beyond: Not for the exam. On a real chip the tail current source is a transistor current mirror, and load resistors are replaced by a mirror too, which is how a CMOS input stage gets gain above 1000 from a 1 V supply; see 5.4. The same current steering runs inside USB, HDMI and optical receivers as CML buffers or differential comparators. Mismatch and offset are studied by Monte Carlo SPICE simulation, not by hand. Search next for gm/ID design methodology, CML driver design, and offset trimming of differential pairs.
